items.prompt: The sun warms a puddle, and the liquid water slowly changes into an invisible gas. What is this change called?
choices: Condensation
Evaporation
Precipitation
Runoff
items.why: The source says the change from liquid to gas is called evaporation.

items.prompt: What happens to water vapor when it cools high above the ground?
choices: It changes into bits of dust in the air.
It soaks into the soil below it.
It changes into tiny drops of liquid water.
It flows downhill into streams and lakes.
items.why: The source says that when water vapor cools, it changes back into tiny drops of liquid water (condensation).

items.prompt: Which list names only kinds of precipitation?
choices: Rain, runoff, sleet and streams
Clouds, dust, hail and snow
Snow, water vapor, rain and puddles
Rain, snow, sleet and hail
items.why: The source says rain, snow, sleet and hail are all precipitation. Each other list has things that are not water falling from clouds.

items.prompt: Rain falls on a hillside. How does some of that water get to where plant roots can take it in?
choices: It soaks into the soil.
It runs off into a river.
It rises with warm air.
It gathers around dust.
items.why: The source says some water soaks into the soil, where plant roots can take it in.

items.prompt: Which sentence best tells what a cloud is?
choices: A large amount of invisible water vapor that has not cooled yet
Bits of dust that warm air has lifted high above the ground
Billions of tiny drops of liquid water gathered around bits of dust
A few big drops of water that are too heavy for the air to hold up
items.why: The source says the tiny liquid drops gather around bits of dust, and billions of them together form a cloud.

items.prompt: On which kind of day would a puddle take the longest to evaporate?
choices: A warm day with a strong wind
A warm day with no wind
A cool day with a strong wind
A cool day with no wind
items.why: The source says evaporation is slower when it is cool and still, so a cool day with no wind is slowest.

items.prompt: Two puddles of the same size form after a storm. Puddle A is in a warm, open spot where the wind blows. Puddle B is in a cool corner where the air is still. Which is most likely true, and why?
choices: Puddle A is gone first, because warm, windy air makes evaporation faster.
Puddle B is gone first, because cool, still air makes evaporation faster.
Both are gone at the same time, because they hold the same amount of water.
Puddle A is gone first, because warm, windy air makes condensation faster.
items.why: Puddles dry up by evaporation, and the source says evaporation is faster when it is warm and windy. The size is the same, so the spot decides it.

items.prompt: On a humid day, the outside of a cold glass gets wet. Which other event in the passage is the same kind of change?
choices: A puddle in the schoolyard slowly drying up in the sun
Water vapor cooling high in the air and forming the drops of a cloud
Drops in a cloud growing heavy and falling to the ground as rain
Rain water flowing downhill over the ground into a stream
items.why: On the glass, water vapor touches something cold and turns to liquid. That is condensation, the same gas-to-liquid change that makes cloud drops when vapor cools high up.

items.prompt: A student says, "When the puddle dried up, that water was used up, so now there is a little less water than before." Which idea from the passage shows the student is wrong?
choices: Clouds make new water to take the place of water that dries up.
Evaporation happens faster on warm days than on cool days.
The water became water vapor, and the same water keeps moving through the cycle.
Some of the water that reaches the ground soaks into the soil.
items.why: The source says the water did not vanish: it changed to water vapor, the same water keeps moving through the steps, and none is used up. It also says no new water is made.

items.prompt: A cloud drifts over the school all morning, but no rain falls from it. From the passage, what is the most likely reason?
choices: Its drops have not joined enough to be too heavy for the air to hold up.
Its water vapor has not cooled enough to change into any drops yet.
Its drops have already soaked into the bits of dust inside the cloud.
Its water has all run off into the streams and lakes below it.
items.why: The source says drops fall only when they join and grow too heavy for the air to hold up. A cloud is already made of drops, so the vapor has cooled; the drops are just still small.
